about: What we know so far about the first step, from someone getting in touch to their application. Shown at kinderform.org/research. Each source says whether a person has checked the claim against the original, when, and against what. Use null for 'not yet checked'. Edit by pull request; tests/validate_findings.py checks the format. A surviving historical check is bound to the unchanged title, summary and source URL by claim_sha256. This guard does not establish a new human review. Clear checked after editing a claim until a person reviews it again.

findings.title: One hub study found quicker visits, without a clear gain in approvals
findings.summary: In the North East of England, councils recruit foster carers together through a regional hub. The reported share with a first visit within 5 days rose from 29% in 2024 to 50% in 2025. A comparison with similar areas found no statistically significant gain in applications or approvals. This does not show that the true effect is zero. The study assessed a whole hub model; it does not isolate reply speed.

findings.title: Some people drop out when one service hands them on to another
findings.summary: The same evaluation found that the hand-over from the hub to the council was a weak point. Some people who withdrew said communication stopped or dropped off, and it was not clear who should answer their questions. The Department for Education now expects hubs that run the whole journey to give each person a named "journey guide" from enquiry to approval.

findings.title: Applications ask far more than enquiry forms, and most UK application forms are not public
findings.summary: In November 2026 we read 52 application forms and packets in 7 countries. A typical UK application form asked 54 questions, against 8 on a typical UK enquiry form. Every UK application form we read asked about health, but none of the 57 UK enquiry forms did. Most UK application forms are not public: of 41 we found, we could read 6. France's national form asks nothing about health or convictions. A medical certificate goes with it, and the council asks for the criminal record itself.

findings.title: Most fostering applications that finish end in withdrawal, not approval
findings.summary: In England, fostering services received 8,290 applications in the year to 31 March 2025. Of the 5,370 applications that finished that year, services approved 2,050 and 3,290 ended in withdrawal. Applicants withdrew 2,175 of these and services withdrew 1,115. That is 61% of finished applications, not of all applications received. Where the applicant withdrew, 20% said the process was not what they expected.

findings.title: How the first contact feels is what people remember
findings.summary: In research for the Department for Education, people mentioned how their first contact felt more than anything else. Many saw getting in touch as the start of an application, and worried about asking "the wrong question". In an online experiment, every redesigned message did better than typical recruitment wording. But that experiment measured what people said they would do, not what they did.

findings.title: Enquiry forms differ a lot in what they ask and what they promise
findings.summary: In November 2026 we read 57 enquiry forms from councils, hubs, independent agencies and adoption agencies across the UK. The shortest asked 3 questions and the longest asked 17. Asking about a spare room depended on the type of service. 8 of the 11 independent agency forms asked about a spare room, but none of the 37 council and hub forms did. Only 7 of the 56 forms where we looked for a reply time said when you would hear back.

findings.title: A named, personal message can change what people do
findings.summary: In a trial at a jobcentre in Bedford, 1,224 jobseekers got a text inviting them to a recruitment event. When the text named their adviser and said a place was booked for them, 26.8% went, against 10.5% for the plainest text. The trial was not about fostering, so the idea needs testing in fostering and adoption before anyone relies on it.

findings.title: Knowing a carer, or simply being asked, starts many people thinking about fostering
findings.summary: A review of research from around the world looked at why people foster. It found that meeting or knowing foster carers is what most often leads people to consider fostering. In an Australian survey of 756 adults, almost 1 in 3 had never considered fostering. They said this was because no one had ever asked them.

findings.title: Some people who go no further say the way the service replied put them off
findings.summary: An Australian study followed up 91 people who had asked about fostering. Only 4% had become carers. The rest split roughly evenly between changes in their own lives and being put off by how the agency responded. The study is old and small, so treat it as a pointer. In the United States, a study of 300 families hoping to adopt from foster care looked at the barriers they met. The families most often reported 3 kinds: the practical steps of the process, how the agency communicated and responded, and emotional support.

findings.title: The relationship with the service shapes whether carers stay
findings.summary: A review of 49 studies looked at why carers keep fostering. It found that the relationship with the agency and support from professionals stand out among the reasons. A Scottish study looked at carers who had stopped fostering. Almost 3 in 5 had stopped because they were unhappy with some part of their fostering service. This is why we treat the first reply as the start of support, not a separate task.

findings.title: Our desk search found no trials of follow-up after a real enquiry
findings.summary: Our November 2026 desk search looked for experiments on reply times, contact attempts, follow-up, contact with experienced carers and hand-offs. We found none with real people asking about fostering or adoption. The search was not a systematic review, so it may have missed studies. The closest study we found was a 2022 online test of message wording. It measured what people said they would do. Kinderform hopes to test these ideas openly, with services' agreement.
